extracted.intended_audience: readers, editors, and distributors of public-domain literary texts (Project Gutenberg users); literary scholars and authors of moral/dialogue works
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit standards drawn from John Bunyan's preface and authorial notes about composing moral/biographical dialogue (form, grounding in observation, concealment of names, use of funeral imagery), together with the Project Gutenberg distribution/editing requirements for reproducing and sharing the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain textual fidelity in scholarly reprints
rubrics_metrics.description: For convenience of reading the old type forms of j, s, u, etc. have been made uniform with those in general modern use; but neither the spelling (including the use of capitals and italics) nor the punctuation has been altered, save as specified. Effect has been given to the errata noted by the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial principle: preserve original orthography and punctuation except where specified; modernize certain letterforms for readability but do not otherwise alter text; record and implement author-noted errata. Use clear editorial statement explaining any normalizations done and the source copy(s) used for reproduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the dialogue form to teach and engage
rubrics_metrics.description: Bunyan: 'I have put it into the form of a Dialogue, that I might with more ease to myself, and pleasure to the Reader, perform the work.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing moral instruction or expositional narrative, consider a conversational/dialogue structure (teacher and questioner) to make doctrines and moral lessons more accessible and lively. Dialogue lets a teacher-character expound while a listener draws out and tests the points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground allegory and moral narratives in observation/fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Bunyan: 'as I said, I have put it forth in this method, yet have I as little as may be, gone out of the road of mine own observation of things... all the things that here I discourse of... have been acted upon the stage of this World, even many times before mine eyes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer basing moral exempla and character sketches on observed behavior and real-life patterns; this increases plausibility and didactic force. Avoid inventing wholly contrived episodes when a truthful account will serve the moral purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace a character's life stages for moral exemplarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Bunyan traces Mr. Badman 'in his Life, from his Childhood to his Death; that thou mayest, as in a Glass, behold with thine own eyes, the steps that take hold of Hell.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show how vice develops into ruin, map the arc of a character across life stages (youth, prime, old age, death). Use cumulative detail to illustrate causal links between habits and final consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid allegorical imagery (e.g., funeral badges) to embody moral judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Bunyan frames Mr. Badman's life as a Funeral, using badges, scutcheons, and funeral pomp to signify the dishonourable character and deserts of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ strong, consistent metaphor/imagery (rituals, funerary motifs, civic symbols) to concretize abstract moral points; align symbolic 'badges' with vices and consequences. But balance vividness with clarity so the allegory communicates rather than obscures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceal or withhold identifying names when publishing censuring accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Bunyan gives reasons for concealing most names: some sins/judgments were private; to avoid provoking relations; to avoid laying persons under additional disgrace. He notes some crimes were public, and only those names he mentions were manifestly notorious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When recounting real sins/punishments, weigh public interest against harm to survivors: omit names for private or ambiguous cases; include names only where the crimes and judgments were public and incontrovertible. Provide stated reasons for any anonymization to justify editorial choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and accept hostile responses when openly rebuking vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Bunyan warns that those of Mr. Badman's kin or friends will likely hate, rail, or condemn the author for exposing wickedness: 'He that reproveth a wicked man, getteth himself a Blot and Shame; but what then? Open rebuke is better than secret love.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers offering moral criticism should expect resistance from those reproved; prioritize the honest admonitory goal over attempts to placate the guilty. Make motives and purposes explicit (e.g., aim to awaken and save) to reduce misunderstanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: awaken, warn, and call to repentance
rubrics_metrics.description: Bunyan explicitly states his aim: 'to detect and condemn the wickedness, warn the evil doer of the Judgment, and fly therefrom myself' and to 'deliver many' from ruin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing didactic fiction or allegory, orient work toward practical ethical/introspective outcomes for readers (awareness, repentance, reform). Ensure narrative devices and rhetorical appeals serve that pastoral/evangelical aim rather than spectacle alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mark notable persons/events in text with marginal indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Bunyan: 'I have pointed at them in the Margent, as with a finger thus:' (graphic of hand pointing) to help readers identify persons referred to elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use marginalia, typographic markers, or annotations to help readers identify whom or what the narrative refers to, especially when employing pseudonyms, typographical conventions, or when referring to earlier passages. Provide legend/explanation for such markers.
